title: Can You Speak English for 40 Seconds? | Improve Your English Speaking | Fluency Practice
short: Can You Speak English for 40 Seconds?

sentences.t: Hello and welcome back to Leo English podcast.
We're very happy you're here with us today.
I'm Tina.
And I'm Leo.
Today, we have a question for you.
Can you speak English for 40 seconds?
40 seconds sounds short until someone asks you to describe your morning.
Exactly. You start with I wake up and suddenly every other word disappears.
Your morning lasts 3 hours, but your English description lasts 3 seconds.
Today, we'll help you build a longer answer without making it complicated.
We'll use ordinary topics, simple words, and examples from our own lives.
You'll learn how to start, add details, give reasons, and finish naturally.
And you'll get several chances to try the challenge yourself.
One important thing first, you don't need to speak without breathing or pausing.
Please breathe. This is English practice, not an underwater competition.
Natural pauses are welcome and mistakes are part of practice.
The goal is to share a clear message, not win a speed contest.
If 40 seconds feels difficult, you can begin with 15 or 20.
We'll show you how to make the challenge work for your level.
If you enjoy learning with us, please like this video and subscribe.
Click the little bell so you can find our next lesson, too.
Get a timer ready if you have one and choose a comfortable place.
You can listen first or join the speaking activities right away.
Ready to discover how much you can say with simple English?
Let's get started.
How are you today, Leo?
I'm good, but I'm suspicious of your timer.
Really? What has the timer done to you?
Last night, I tried talking about my breakfast for 40 seconds.
That sounds like useful preparation.
How did it go?
I said, "I eat toast, I drink coffee, and I like breakfast."
And then?
Then I looked at the timer and only 8 seconds passed.
So, you still had plenty of time to describe the toast.
Exactly, but I didn't know my toast well enough.
You could describe when you eat, where you sit, or why you choose it.
I understand that now, but last night the toast felt very private.
What did you do this weekend apart from interviewing your breakfast?
On Saturday, I met my cousin at a small cafe near the station.
Nice. What time did you meet?
Around 11, and we stayed for about an hour and a half.
What did you talk about?
Work, family, and a terrible film we both watched recently.
That sounds like an easy conversation to continue.
It was because we had strong opinions and enough sandwiches.
Did you do anything on Sunday?
I went grocery shopping, washed some clothes, and tried the speaking challenge.
So, your weekend included social time, practical tasks, and English practice.
Yes, although the laundry conversation was much longer than the breakfast conversation.
You talked about laundry?
I had questions, Tina.
Why do socks leave relationships so suddenly?
I'm afraid that topic is outside today's lesson.
Fair enough. What did you do this weekend?
On Saturday, I visited my sister and helped her organize a bookshelf.
You actually enjoy organizing things, don't you?
I do, especially when there's tea and someone interesting to talk to.
How long did you stay?
About 2 hours, and then we went for a short walk.
That sounds calm.
My cousin and I organized nothing except another coffee order.
Both weekends give us useful things to describe in English.
True. Neither of us climbed a mountain or met a famous person.
And neither activity is necessary for an interesting answer.
Speaking of answers, I notice you keep asking small follow-up questions.
Yes. Each question gives you another part of the story to explain.
Who, where, when, and why.
Suddenly, my eight-second answer grows.
Exactly. Today, we'll learn how to ask yourself those questions while speaking.
Good. I'm ready to give my toast a second chance.
Let's begin with the purpose of this challenge, sharing one clear idea for around 40 seconds.
We're not testing how many words you know, and we're not counting every mistake.
That already feels better.
When I hear challenge, I imagine someone checking my grammar with a red pen.
I prefer a friendly challenge with no angry stationery.
Think of the timer as a guide, not a judge.
It helps you notice whether you give yourself enough space to explain something instead of stopping after one short sentence.
So, if I finish a clear answer at 35 seconds, that isn't a disaster.
And if I need 45 seconds, the English police don't arrive.
Exactly. Now, choose a familiar topic, such as your breakfast, your neighborhood, or your favorite day.
Familiar means you already know the subject from your own life.
Wait, what does familiar mean again?
Is it the same as easy?
My family is familiar to me, but explaining my family can become complicated very quickly.
Familiar means known, not necessarily easy.
For this activity, choose something both familiar and fairly simple, like one person in your family, rather than your entire family history.
That makes sense.
I can describe my cousin's coffee habit without explaining three generations of family decisions.
A smaller topic gives my brain a clear place to start.
Before learning the method, try a first attempt.
Your question is, "What do you usually do in the evening?"
Start with what you normally do, and continue naturally.
I usually eat dinner, watch something, and go to bed.
That's my answer, and I can already hear how short it is.
My whole evening has disappeared into three activities.
That answer is a useful beginning, not a failure.
You already have three ideas, so now we can develop them.
Develop means make something fuller by adding useful information.
Oh, so we don't throw the answer away, we keep it and add things, like improving soup.
Although, I should probably stop comparing every lesson to food.
Here's our speaking map.
Answer, details, reason, ending.
First, answer directly.
Next, describe something specific.
Then, explain why it matters.
Finally, close the idea naturally.
Four parts sounds manageable.
I don't need four beautiful paragraphs, do I?
I just need a few connected thoughts that help the listener understand my answer.
Exactly. We can use usually to start, for example, to add detail, and because to explain a reason.
A simple ending might be, "That's why I enjoy it."
Let me try the beginning again.
In the evening, I usually eat dinner around 7:00 and watch a comedy.
That already gives us a time and a preference.
Good. Now, describe where you are or who you're with, then explain your choice.
What makes that evening pleasant for you?
And is every evening exactly the same?
Usually, I'm at home and sometimes my cousin comes over.
I choose comedies because I want something light after work.
On Fridays, though, I sometimes meet friends for dinner instead.
Excellent. You add a normal routine, a reason, and one small difference.
Notice that none of those details needs difficult vocabulary, but together, they make the answer more personal.
I see. The secret isn't speaking slowly until the timer gives up.
The secret is having enough real information to share while keeping the language simple.
Here's a fuller model.
Most evenings, I get home around 6:00, make a simple dinner, and sit down to eat by 7:00.
After that, I usually watch a comedy or call my cousin, especially when work feels tiring.
I prefer quiet evenings because they give me time to relax and enjoy my own space.
On Fridays though, I sometimes meet friends for dinner instead, so my routine changes a little.
Overall, my evenings are simple, but I enjoy that balance.
That sounds complete, and you stay on one topic.
You don't suddenly describe your childhood or your neighbor's bicycle.
I can follow every part without working too hard.
Exactly. Now, listeners, pause the episode and try your own evening answer with a 40-second timer.
Natural pauses are fine.
When you return, we'll explore what to do if you finish early.
Before you pause, choose just three notes: time, activity, and reason.
Don't write a full speech, and don't worry if the first attempt feels messy.
This is a starting point.
Welcome back. If your answer ends early, ask yourself one follow-up question: when, where, who, how often, or why.
Choose the question that adds something useful to your topic.
For my breakfast answer, why gives me I eat toast because it's quick.
When gives me I usually eat at 7:30.
My toast now has a schedule.
Exactly. And how often gives you useful frequency language.
You can say every morning, three times a week, or only on weekends, depending on what is true for you.
I sometimes say three time a week when I rush.
It should be three times a week, right?
I need the plural because there are three occasions.
Correct. During a speaking attempt though, don't restart your whole answer over one small error.
Make a brief correction if it helps, then continue with your message.
So, I can say three time three times a week and move forward.
I don't need to apologize to the listener, the microphone, and the English language.
Exactly. Let's practice another question.
What is a place you enjoy visiting?
Choose a real place, describe one or two features, and explain what you do there.
I choose the cafe near the station.
It has six small tables, a window seat, and excellent sandwiches.
I go there about twice a month, usually with my cousin.
Those details create a clear picture.
Now give your reason, and perhaps one honest limitation.
A place can be enjoyable without being perfect, which often makes the answer more natural.
I like it because the staff are friendly and nobody rushes us.
It gets noisy after 12, though, so we usually arrive earlier.
Good. You use though to introduce a small contrast, meaning a difference from the main positive idea.
You can also use but, which is simple and clear.
I prefer but when I'm nervous because it comes quickly.
I like learning new expressions, but I don't want to test six unfamiliar words during one speaking challenge.
I agree. Use language you can manage, then add new language during review.
A speaking attempt and a vocabulary experiment don't always need to happen at the same time.
That's helpful. Sometimes I try to sound advanced and forget how to finish my sentence.
A sandwich becomes a complex bread-based experience, and then everyone needs a break.
Let's talk about missing words.
If you forget the exact word, describe the object or action instead.
This is called paraphrasing, expressing an idea in another way.
What does paraphrasing mean in everyday terms?
If I forget kettle, can I say the thing I use to boil water?
That's longer, but people understand.
Yes, that's a good example.
You can also use a category, such as a kitchen tool, followed by its purpose.
The goal is to communicate, not hide every vocabulary gap.
I once forgot balcony while describing an apartment.
I said, "The little outside space next to the living room."
And my friend understood immediately.
The conversation continued perfectly well.
That's a useful learning experience.
Now, let's discuss pauses.
A short pause can help you choose your next idea, breathe comfortably, or separate two parts of your answer.
I'm glad you say that because speak for 40 seconds sounds like never stop making sound.
I don't want to turn into a kettle myself.
No, pauses belong in speech.
If you need a moment, use one honest phrase such as, "Let me think."
But don't fill every space with the same expression.
So, I can pause after describing the cafe, then explain why I like it.
That pause has a purpose, unlike saying "basically" seven times while looking frightened.
Exactly. Your pace matters, too.
Pace means how quickly or slowly you speak.
Choose a comfortable pace that lets the listener understand you without making you feel rushed.
I naturally speed up when I'm excited.
Then, I forget an idea and slow down suddenly, like a bus with a confused driver.
A steady pace sounds much better.
Let's try a model for me.
One place I enjoy visiting is a small park about 10 minutes from my apartment.
I usually go there on Sunday mornings when the paths are quiet and there's plenty of space.
Sometimes, I walk for half an hour, and sometimes I sit near the trees with a book.
I like the park because I can leave my phone in my bag and enjoy the fresh air.
It's a simple place, but I usually feel calmer afterward.
I notice you give a distance, a time, two activities, and feeling.
Those details help the answer grow without repeating "I like the park" again and again.
Exactly. Repeating the main idea once is fine, but repeating it several times doesn't add much.
Instead, add an example, a reason, a comparison, or a small difference.
For example, I prefer this park to the one near the station because it's quieter.
That adds a comparison and keeps me on the same topic.
Good. Now listeners, your second challenge is a place you enjoy visiting.
Pause the episode, take 10 seconds to choose three keywords, and then try speaking for 40 seconds.
Choose somewhere ordinary if you want.
A library, a shop, a relative's home, or a local street.
You don't need a famous place to give a good answer.
Welcome back. Let's think about preparation.
Three keywords can guide you, but a full written answer can make you depend on reading.
Try notes such as Sunday, trees, peaceful.
I disagree a little because a full script feels safer at first.
What if someone can't begin with keywords yet?
A blank page can feel surprisingly loud.
That's a fair point.
Beginners can write a short answer first, read it aloud, and then reduce it to keywords.
The next step is to speak without reading every word.
I like that.
We build support and then slowly remove it rather than pretending everyone starts in the same place.
I'll keep my three notes, but lose the 12-page breakfast report.
Another helpful choice is a topic with a clear order, like making lunch.
You can use first, then, after that, and finally to explain the process.
Let me try.
First, I check the fridge and decide what to cook.
Then I wash the vegetables and prepare some rice.
Already I know what comes next.
Exactly. Continue with one specific detail and a reason, rather than listing every movement.
You might explain how long it takes or why you choose that meal.
The whole meal usually takes about 20 minutes, which is useful after work.
I like it because it's simple and I can use the vegetables I already have.
That works well.
Now remember that grammar follows the meaning.
Use present forms for routines, past forms for finished events, and suitable future forms for plans.
So, I say, "I usually cook at home."
for a habit, but for last Sunday, I say, "I cooked at home."
not "I cook last Sunday."
Correct. We don't need to force every topic into the present tense.
Choose a routine today if you want simpler practice, then try a past experience when you feel ready.
That helps. Last weekend, I made soup and forgot the salt, so there's a real story available.
It was healthy, technically, but it tasted like warm water with ambitions.
A short past story can follow three parts: what happened, what you did, and how you felt.
You don't need to tell your entire weekend to make it interesting.
Last Sunday, I made vegetable soup for lunch, but I forgot the salt.
I noticed after the first spoonful, added some, and tried again.
I felt relieved because the problem was easy to fix.
That's a clear short version.
To develop it, add who was there or why you were cooking, but only if the extra detail supports the story.
My cousin was coming over, and I wanted to make something warm because it was raining.
Good. Now, the soup has a situation instead of being lonely in a pot.
Let's discuss a common difficulty: running out of ideas before 40 seconds.
Usually, the answer doesn't need a new topic.
It needs one deeper question about the current topic.
So, if I'm discussing music, I don't suddenly start describing buses.
I ask myself, "When do I listen?"
or "How does this music make me feel?"
Exactly. You can also imagine a curious listener asking, "Can you give me an example?"
An example turns a general statement into something real and easier to explain.
If I say, "Music helps me relax."
my example is, "I often play quiet songs while I wash the dishes after dinner."
That's much clearer than just saying relaxing twice.
Now, let's consider the opposite problem, too many ideas.
Select one main point and two supporting details, then finish.
More information isn't always more helpful to the listener.
That problem belongs to me.
I start with music and somehow describe my cousin's haircut, a train journey, and an argument about cheese.
I need a smaller map.
Here's a useful ending.
That's why I enjoy it.
Or, overall, it works well for me.
Don't keep adding sentences just because you're afraid to stop.
And if the timer rings while I'm finishing a thought, I can finish the sentence naturally.
I don't need to stop in the middle of because like a broken recording.
Right. The timer helps you practice.
It doesn't control every word.
In this activity, completing a clear thought matters more than stopping at exactly 40.0 seconds.
That makes the challenge feel much more human.
I'm learning to speak to a person, not perform a perfect relationship with a stopwatch.
Let's move to preferences, which offer a simple structure: choice, reason, example, and small contrast.
Your question is, do you prefer mornings or evenings?
I prefer evenings because I feel more awake and have fewer tasks waiting.
For example, after dinner, I can listen to music or call a friend.
Mornings are useful, but evenings feel more like my own time.
Good. And you can add one honest limitation, such as staying up too late.
That creates a balanced answer without changing the topic or using complicated language.
The only problem is that I sometimes stay up later than I plan, so I try to turn off my phone around 10:30.
That gives the answer a natural finish.
My preference is different.
I prefer mornings because the house is quiet and my mind feels fresh.
Most days, I make tea around 7:00 and spend a few minutes reading before work.
I also like checking my schedule then because I can choose one important task without feeling rushed.
Evenings are pleasant, too, but I sometimes feel too tired to concentrate.
For me, a calm morning is a useful start to the day.
Different answers, same useful structure.
I also hear that you don't claim mornings are best for everyone.
You explain your own preference, which makes the answer feel honest.
Exactly. Now it's your third challenge, listeners.
Mornings or evenings?
Pause and speak for 40 seconds using a reason and a real example from your life.
If you prefer both, explain that, too.
You might say, "I enjoy mornings on weekends, but evenings are easier during the week."
You don't need a dramatic opinion.
Welcome back. How do we review an attempt?
Ask three questions.
Is my main idea clear?
Do I add useful details?
And can I understand my own recording?
Not, "Do I sound exactly like Tina?"
Or, "Do I use 11 advanced words?"
Those questions don't help me explain my actual life any better.
Correct. If you record yourself, choose just one thing to improve next time.
Maybe you need a clearer beginning, a slower pace, or one example after your reason.
I prefer checking one thing because checking everything makes me tired.
I once listened to a recording five times and only noticed how strange my voice sounded.
Many people find recorded voices unfamiliar at first.
You can focus on the message instead of judging the sound of your voice, and recording is optional for this practice.
That's useful. If recording makes someone uncomfortable today, they can just speak and reflect afterward.
The important thing is actually trying, not buying equipment or creating a studio.
Let's build a short practice routine.
Choose a topic, prepare three key words, and speak once.
Then, review one point, try again, and compare the two attempts.
Two attempts sound enough for one session.
I don't want to repeat until I hate my own breakfast.
I'd rather improve a little and come back tomorrow.
That's sensible.
Repeating the same topic lets you focus on expressing familiar ideas, but later you can change the question slightly, so you're not only memorizing one answer.
For example, first I describe my breakfast, and later I explain my favorite weekend meal.
Some language stays useful, but I need to make new choices.
Exactly. Also, longer doesn't automatically mean better.
A clear 30-second answer can communicate more than 40 seconds of repeated phrases.
Use the challenge to develop ideas, not collect seconds.
I'm glad you say that.
Otherwise, I might spend the final 10 seconds saying, "Breakfast is good.
Very good. Really good."
My toast deserves better communication.
If 40 seconds is too difficult, begin with 20, then add one detail.
If it feels easy, try a less familiar topic or include a reasoned comparison.
So, the challenge can grow without becoming a punishment.
20 seconds today is a starting point, not proof that someone is bad at English.
Exactly. Let's finish with one fresh question.
What is one small habit you enjoy?
I'll give you a moment to choose, and then you can model an answer.
One small habit I enjoy is taking a short walk after dinner, especially when the weather is cool.
I usually leave home around 7:30 and walk for about 20 minutes near my apartment.
Sometimes I listen to music, but often I leave my headphones at home and notice what's around me.
I like this habit because it gives me a break from screens and a quiet end to the day.
It's simple, it costs nothing, and it's easy to fit into my evening.
That's a complete answer with a habit, timing, details, and a reason.
Your language stays simple, and every sentence gives the listener something useful, rather than filling space.
I feel the difference now.
I'm not trying to survive 40 empty seconds.
I'm sharing a small part of my life with a clear beginning and ending.
That is the heart of this lesson.
Choose a familiar topic, add meaningful details, and speak at a comfortable pace with permission to pause and make small mistakes.
And if the toast still refuses to cooperate, choose a different topic.
You have a whole life to talk about, and your first answer doesn't need to be your best one.
You know, Leo, while we were talking, we used many useful words.
Let's look at 10 of them and connect each one to your speaking practice.
Good. My timer can rest while my vocabulary gets some exercise.
First word, familiar.
This means something you know or recognize because you meet it often.
We choose a familiar topic, like our home or our breakfast.
Exactly. For example, this street feels familiar because I walk here every day.
And you can also say, I feel more comfortable talking about familiar places.
Notice the phrase familiar with.
You can say, I'm familiar with this neighborhood.
So, familiar with means I know something, not that it's part of my family.
Right. What familiar topic feels easiest for you to describe?
Food, because I think about it several times a day.
Next word, develop.
This means make an idea fuller or more complete.
We develop an answer instead of throwing away the first sentence.
Exactly. For example, she develops her idea by giving a personal example.
And you can also say, I want to develop this short answer.
In In lesson, developing an answer doesn't mean making it complicated.
It means adding something useful, like a reason or a time.
Which part of your evening answer do you want to develop?
The part about watching comedies because I can explain what I enjoy.
Next word, detail.
This is a small piece of information about something.
Like the six tables in my favorite cafe.
Yes. For example, one useful detail is the time the shop opens.
And I add a detail about the friend who joins me.
A detail can answer who, where, when, or how often.
So, details help the listener imagine the situation more clearly.
What kind of detail do you naturally remember?
I remember what people eat, but I sometimes forget their arrival time.
Next word, pace.
This means the speed at which something happens.
In our conversation, we use it for speaking speed.
Exactly. For example, she speaks at a comfortable pace during the lesson.
And I slow my pace when my words become unclear.
A fast pace isn't always better, and a slow pace isn't always worse.
The useful question is whether the listener can follow me.
What happens to your pace when you feel nervous?
I speed up, so I remind myself to breathe between ideas.
Next word, pause.
This means stop briefly before continuing.
Not give up completely, just stop for a moment.
Right. For example, I pause before I explain the main reason.
And a short pause gives me time to choose my next idea.
Pause can be a noun or a verb.
Take a pause or pause briefly.
I also hear take a short break for a longer rest.
Yes. Where does a pause help in your speaking?
Between my example and my ending because I can finish more calmly.
Next word, paraphrase.
This means express an idea in different words.
We use it when the exact word disappears.
Exactly. For example, I paraphrase the instructions so my friend understands it.
And when I forget a word, I paraphrase instead of stopping.
A good paraphrase keeps the important meaning even when the wording changes.
So it isn't simply replacing one word with any other word.
What object can you describe without naming it?
An umbrella. Something I hold over my head when it rains.
Next word, keyword.
This means an important word that helps you remember an idea.
We prepare three keywords, not a whole page of sentences.
Right. For example, my first keyword is Saturday because it reminds me of the event.
And three keywords help me remember the order of my answer.
Write enough to guide yourself, but not so much that you only read.
A keyword is a reminder, not a complete answer.
What three keywords fit your walking habit?
Dinner, 20 minutes, screens.
I can build the answer from those.
Next word, contrast.
This means a difference between two things or ideas.
We use a contrast when we compare mornings and evenings.
Exactly. For example, I enjoy busy cafes, but my sister prefers quiet ones.
And there's a clear contrast between my weekday and weekend routines.
Words like but and however can introduce a contrast.
I usually choose but because it feels easy and natural.
What contrast can you make about your favorite cafe?
It's quiet before lunch, but it gets noisy in the afternoon.
Next word, review.
This means look at something again to check or improve it.
We review one part of our answer after the first attempt.
Yes. For example, I review my notes before I start speaking.
And we review the recording to check whether the message is clear.
Review doesn't mean criticize everything or search for every possible mistake.
That's important because I sometimes turn a review into an argument with myself.
What do you want to review first?
My beginning because a clear first sentence helps me feel settled.
Final word, attempt.
This means a try at doing something.
So my first attempt can be short and still count.
Exactly. For example, her second attempt includes a clearer example.
And I feel less nervous after my first attempt.
We say make an attempt or simply try depending on the sentence.
And we don't need to call an imperfect attempt a failure.
What do you learn from your breakfast attempt?
I learn that I need details, not a more exciting breakfast.
Let's finish with a quick vocabulary summary.
Familiar, known or recognized because you meet it often.
Develop, make an idea fuller or more complete.
Detail, a small piece of information.
Pace, the speed of an activity or of speech.
Pause, a brief stop before continuing.
Paraphrase, express an idea using different words.
Keyword, an important word that reminds you of an idea.
Contrast, a difference between two things or ideas.
Review, look at something again to check or improve it.
Attempt, a try at doing something.
Okay, Leo. That was a lot of talking about speaking for 40 seconds.
Yes, we spend much longer explaining 40 seconds than 40 seconds.
That's because we're learning a method you can use many times.
Good point. My toast, coffee, and evening walk all get something from it.
Let's think about what we learned in five clear sections.
Five sections sound good.
My memory appreciates a small organized group.
First, we learned what the challenge really means.
You try to explain one idea for around 40 seconds with natural pauses and clear language.
It doesn't mean speaking at top speed or making sound constantly.
Exactly. We use phrases like I usually, one place I enjoy, and I prefer to begin with a direct answer.
And if 40 seconds feels too difficult, 20 seconds is a useful start.
Then we talked about choosing a topic and preparing a small map.
Familiar subjects are helpful because you already know the information.
My home, my meals, my evening routine, or a place I enjoy visiting.
Our map is answer, details, reason, and ending.
You can prepare three keywords to remind you of those ideas.
For example, Sunday, park, peaceful gives me something clear to build.
After that, we learned how to develop an answer.
We ask small questions.
When, where, who, how often, and why.
I go walking becomes I walk near my apartment for 20 minutes after dinner.
Exactly. Then a reason adds another useful layer.
I like it because I get a break from screens.
We also use examples and comparisons instead of repeating the same idea.

If you forget a word, paraphrase.
If you need a moment, pause.
If you make a small error, continue.
We use phrases like, let me think, or what I mean is, when they help.

Finally, we learned how to review and try again.
Choose one point to improve, such as a clearer reason or a more comfortable pace.
Not 10 things at once, and not a complete investigation into my voice.
A second attempt gives you a chance to make a small change.
Then later, we change the question so we can use the language differently.
Remember our main example.
One habit, a few details, a reason, and a natural ending.
That's much more useful than 40 seconds of it's good, really good.
Exactly. The method is simple, even if it takes practice to feel comfortable.
Choose something real, tell us a little more, and give your thought an ending.
You don't need a perfect story or an exciting life event.
An ordinary evening already gives you plenty to talk about.
Now, we want to hear from you.
This is our favorite part.
You listened to our answers, and now we want to learn about yours.

I like that question because everyone can choose something different.
I'll answer first.
I choose my Sunday morning walk because I can describe the place, the time, and how I feel afterward.
That gives you several clear parts without needing a complicated story.
Exactly. My three keywords are morning, trees, and calm.
My answer is different.
I choose my favorite cafe because I know it well and can describe the food, the people, and the atmosphere.

Years of personal study finally become useful.
See? We have different answers, and that's okay.
A quiet walk in a busy cafe both work for speaking practice.

I choose it because blank."

Your shopping routine is enough.
